contexts.title: The bill’s route to a binding first contract
contexts.html:
The bill covers bargaining for a first contract after a union is newly recognized or certified. If there is no agreement 90 days after bargaining starts, either side may ask for mediation from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS): “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [1] A mediator cannot decide the dispute. If there is still no agreement 30 days after that request, the dispute goes to arbitration, where a panel decides: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].

The panel has “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [1] If a side does not choose its member, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1] The panel majority’s decision binds both sides for two years unless both agree in writing to change it. Either waiting period can be longer only if both sides agree.

Under the law in force on June 9, 2026, there is no such route. The duty to bargain “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [2].

The panel route applies only to a first contract, not to later contracts. The bill sets no deadline for the panel’s decision: “it does not limit the timeline of arbitration.” [3]

Under current law, neither side has to agree to anything. Under the bill, either side can start the route to a panel after the waiting periods, and neither side can stop the panel by refusing to choose its member. More time needs both sides’ agreement.

contexts.title: What the panel must weigh
contexts.html:
The panel’s decision must be based on five factors: the employer’s financial status and prospects; the size and type of its business; employees’ cost of living; “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [1]; and what other employers in the same business provide. The bill gives no order of priority.

These factors tell the panel what to consider. They do not state what the panel must award. They name no particular contract terms and set no pay level.

contexts.title: Current terms stay in place until an agreement
contexts.html:
Under existing law, upon reaching a good-faith impasse, “the NLRA entitles an employer to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer.” [1] The bill adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2].

Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe reads this duty as one that “extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.” [3] He adds that it “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” [3]

This reading comes from law-firm analyses, not a court ruling. The duty keeps both good and bad current terms, so it can stop an employer from either cutting them or raising them on its own. The sources give no figure for how often employers make such changes today.

contexts.title: The duty to bargain lasts until an election removes the union
contexts.html:
Under the bill, “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1].

Under existing law, an employer can announce, before a contract ends, that it will withdraw recognition “upon receiving objective evidence that the union has actually lost majority support.” [2] The union may then file, “within 45 days from the date of that announcement, an election petition” [3]. “If no such petition is timely filed, the employer may rely on the disaffection evidence to affect withdrawal.” [3] In the labor board’s words, “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” [4]. The bill ends that option, so an election is needed even where the union has not asked for one. Workers keep the right to vote a union out: Section 9 allows a petition “by an employee or group of employees” [5], followed by “an election by secret ballot” [5] when the labor board finds a question about representation.

This applies to the general duty to bargain, not only to first contracts. Existing law already protects newly certified unions for 12 months. These facts bear on how often the change matters.

contexts.title: New required work for a reduced federal mediation agency
contexts.html:
The bill adds required mediation and panel-appointment duties for the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) and provides no added funding. A former labor-board chair wrote that the requirement “would presumably significantly increase the demand for the FMCS’s services” [1]. FMCS reports it “limited its involvement to facilities that provide health care services with bargaining units of 250 or more members, and to bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction.” [2] Lawyers warn: “The FMCS does not have anywhere near the personnel to meet the obligations this legislation would impose upon it.” [3] A June 12 account from the State of Connecticut about the 2025 cuts says that “the majority of the federal agency’s employees have not returned.” [4]

Accounts of the agency’s service limits differ between sources, and one demand statement was written in March 2025 about an earlier version of the proposal. FMCS already mediates initial contract negotiations, so the added burden is the work beyond that. The sources describe demand and staff limits, not how the agency would divide its work.

blocks.html: The federal mediation agency’s current limits challenge the claim that this route is usable for small groups of workers. Its proposed service form, published May 15, 2026, says of first-contract cases: “These cases will be assigned to a mediator if they meet the current criteria/metrics for case assignment.” [3] A supporter of the bill names the condition: “Without a robust, government-supported mediation and arbitration system, the Faster Labor Contracts Act would not be able to live up to its promise.” [4] Stopping an employer from blocking appointments does not solve this service gap. This does not show the route is unavailable: the bill’s duty has no size limit, and the time before referral runs from the request. The sources document limits under current practice, not how the agency would carry out the new duty for small groups.

AFT’s bargaining resolution on this coverage dates from 2017; its site notes that older resolutions may not reflect current policy, and its 2025 resolution separately supports coverage. After an overall impasse, employers generally may impose a final offer, and a union can break the impasse by showing that resumed bargaining might be fruitful; the bill instead keeps current terms until an agreement. The sources do not settle whether the Religious Freedom Restoration Act applies to an award by this panel.

blocks.html: Contracts can fund changes in how work is done. Minneapolis janitors won “Funding for a green cleaning initiative to reduce waste and water and energy consumption while transitioning away from toxic chemicals, with the goal of significantly lowering carbon emissions from buildings.” [15] Winning it took trade-offs: “We ultimately won, but had to compromise on the amount of funding and sacrifice other issues like additional holidays that were important to groups of the members.” [15] None of the panel’s five factors requires pollution reductions. A panel could settle a first contract without pollution-reducing terms that workers would insist on before approving it, and workers could not reject that result by a vote.

The example shows green terms and bargaining trade-offs, not a first-contract vote the bill would bypass. The panel factors can accommodate green work methods even though they do not require pollution cuts.

blocks.html: A member vote does not always decide the outcome today: after a real deadlock, an employer may put into effect terms consistent with offers the union rejected. Under the bill, current terms stay in place until an agreement, and the union chooses one of three panel members. These facts narrow what workers lose. They do not restore their power to refuse a panel-set contract that lacks pollution-reducing terms.

blocks.html: Where an employer has evidence that most workers no longer support the union, and the union has not asked for an election in time, existing rules let the employer withdraw recognition after the contract ends. In this situation the bill adds a required vote where the union has not asked for one: workers keep collective representation until an election removes it.

source_refs.quote: So in this situation the bill adds a required vote where the union has not asked for one.
Workers keep collective representation until an election removes it.

blocks.html: The bill itself states how delay can weaken a workers’ group: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer” [1]. Talks must start “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” [1], “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” [1], and the duty to bargain continues until an election removes the union. These rules strengthen workers’ chance to have their chosen group heard despite management’s opposition.

blocks.html: Existing law already requires good-faith bargaining. The added rules concern when talks start and how long the representative keeps its role. A stronger bargaining role does not by itself show greater acceptance or understanding of different people. This does not answer the separate route about cooperation across racial lines.

blocks.html: Workers use the existing withdrawal process. A June 2025 report describes a Sunoco driver named Fifer who gathered majority support against the union: “Fifer opted to submit his petition to his employer, who withdrew recognition from the USW union in accordance with the Johnson Controls decision.” [7] Union representation covers people who disagree: the union bargains “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit over wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” [8]. Under the bill, clear majority opposition, even when expressed independently, would no longer end the bargaining duty; workers would have to wait for an election.

The labor-board account calls an election “the preferred method for determining employees’ representational preferences.” [2] A secret ballot lets workers make a final choice without others knowing it, “insulating them from retaliation from whichever side they fail to support.” [9] Employer withdrawal can be quicker, but speed alone does not establish that confirming the majority’s wishes is unfair.

blocks.html: The existing process is an employer’s power, not a vote workers can themselves use to remove the union. Workers can take their changed wishes to the labor board without depending on the employer, and the board “shall direct an election by secret ballot and shall certify the results thereof.” [5] An election tests the workforce’s current choice, including the views of workers who did not sign the petition. Losing the employer’s option is not shown to mean less listening to, or acceptance of, workers who reject the union.

nodes.title: More first contracts, or earlier ones
nodes.claim_html: Because a dispute referred to a panel must end in a binding decision, at least some new unions would get a first contract that they would otherwise lack or would get later.

nodes.title: Concern: a way past an employer’s delay
nodes.claim_html: A usable way to settle the contract, without first persuading the stronger side, makes the right to bargain usable for workers with less power. That protects people with less power and supports just treatment.

nodes.title: Conservation staff
nodes.claim_html: Some newly organized staff at conservation groups would gain pay, benefits or training through added or earlier first contracts, helping those groups keep and attract the staff who protect wildlife and habitats. Pay gains need the pay claim; benefits or training need the claim about non-pay contract terms.

nodes.title: Nature: conservation staff
nodes.claim_html: Supporting the staff who protect wildlife and habitats serves protecting nature.

nodes.title: Easing energy workers’ fear of poor pay in clean energy
nodes.claim_html: In clean-energy workplaces that newly form unions, a binding way to settle wages and benefits would ease part of some energy workers’ fear of poor pay and benefits, and so build some support among them for moving to cleaner energy.

nodes.title: Nature: support for moving to cleaner energy
nodes.claim_html: Building energy workers’ support for reducing the emissions that harm nature serves protecting the natural environment from pollution.

nodes.title: A base for environmental campaigns
nodes.claim_html: By limiting first-contract delay, the bill would help some new unions last that workers can use for environmental campaigns.

nodes.title: Nature: a base for environmental campaigns
nodes.claim_html: Keeping open a way into environmental campaigns serves taking part in protecting nature.

nodes.title: Stronger unions that resist pollution controls
nodes.claim_html: Added or earlier first contracts would give some unions in fossil-fuel industries a firmer membership and dues base, strengthening organized resistance to pollution controls.

nodes.title: Nature: unions that resist pollution controls
nodes.claim_html: Stronger organized resistance to pollution controls works against protecting the natural environment from pollution.

nodes.title: Enforceable terms other than pay
nodes.claim_html: Some of the added or earlier first contracts would contain written terms, other than pay levels, that workers can enforce and would otherwise lack or get later. This does not say which terms any one contract would contain, or that the contracts would be better for workers overall.

nodes.title: Health coverage in contracts
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would add or bring forward health coverage, or lower the share of health costs workers pay themselves.

nodes.title: Paid sick leave in contracts
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would add or bring forward paid sick leave.

nodes.title: Paid parental leave in contracts
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would add or bring forward paid parental leave.

nodes.title: Pensions or other paid leave in contracts
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would add or bring forward pensions, or paid leave other than sick or parental leave.

nodes.title: Concern: health coverage, paid leave or retirement income
nodes.claim_html: Access to care, paid leave or retirement income, any one of which is enough, protects people at vulnerable stages of life and those who depend on their care. Each of the four benefit claims is a separate route.

nodes.title: Personal Security: health coverage
nodes.claim_html: Health coverage in more contracts, and sooner, lowers a cost barrier to medical care. That serves avoiding disease and protecting health.

nodes.title: Personal Security: paid sick leave
nodes.claim_html: Paid sick leave in more contracts, and sooner, supports treatment and recovery and reduces exposure to sick workers, whether as a worker, coworker, customer or patient.

nodes.title: Tradition: paid parental leave
nodes.claim_html: With paid parental leave in more first contracts, parents who observe the religious rule against abortion face less work and income pressure in continuing that observance.

nodes.title: Posted schedules and advance notice
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would require posting schedules or giving advance notice of schedules and changes, so workers can plan their time.

nodes.title: Schedule adjustments for religious holidays
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would let workers request schedule changes to observe religious holidays.

nodes.title: Concern: predictable hours for caregivers
nodes.claim_html: Predictable hours protect caregivers’ income and their opportunities to work.

nodes.title: Tradition: time for worship
nodes.claim_html: Protected Sunday and holiday arrangements, or new religious-holiday and advance-notice rules that let families plan regular worship and teaching, either one, serve keeping Christian customs and teaching them to children. The first route needs only the duty to keep current terms. The advance-notice route needs the claim about posted schedules and notice, and the religious-holiday route needs the claim about schedule adjustments.

nodes.title: Shared pay rules less open to bias
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would set shared pay rules, such as published pay schedules, that make pay less open to bias against women and racial minorities. This is about how pay is set, not whether pay rises.

nodes.title: Concern: pay rules less open to bias
nodes.claim_html: Shared pay rules that reduce unequal treatment support fair treatment and equal opportunities regardless of race or gender.

nodes.title: Posted job openings
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would require posting job openings and set out how workers can seek promotions.

nodes.title: Concern: posted job openings
nodes.claim_html: Knowing what openings exist and how to seek them supports equal opportunities.

nodes.title: Training and tuition help
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would provide job training or help with tuition.

nodes.title: Concern: training and tuition help
nodes.claim_html: Training or help with tuition gives workers whose own resources limit their choices a way to build skills. That serves equal opportunities in life.

nodes.title: Limits on outside labor
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would limit moving union-represented work to temporary staff, outside companies or managers.

nodes.title: Concern: limits on replacing work with outside labor
nodes.claim_html: Limits on replacing their work with outside labor give workers a way to defend the jobs their households rely on. This protects people who are vulnerable to losing their income.

nodes.title: Hospital staffing rules
nodes.claim_html: Some first contracts at private hospitals would set enforceable nurse-staffing rules that keep staffing closer to safe levels for patients.

nodes.title: Personal Security: hospital staffing
nodes.claim_html: If more first contracts in private hospitals include staffing rules, patients get safer staffing. That gives a personal health reason for anyone who may need hospital care.

nodes.title: Terms that adapt work to differences
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would contain practical terms that adapt work to people’s differences.

nodes.title: Regular discussion across differences
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would set up regular workplace discussion or training about differences between people.

nodes.title: Tolerance: regular discussion across differences
nodes.claim_html: Turning proposals for continuing discussion and learning into workplace rules serves listening to and understanding people who are different.

nodes.title: Enforceable safety rules
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would contain worker-safety rules that workers can enforce and would otherwise lack or get later.

nodes.title: Concern: enforceable safety protection
nodes.claim_html: Concern for people exposed to harm at work favors giving them safety protection they can enforce.

nodes.title: Personal Security: enforceable safety protection
nodes.claim_html: Getting and enforcing protection from hazards at work, sooner, serves avoiding injury and illness at work.

nodes.title: From care-worker protections to national outbreak capacity
nodes.claim_html: Infection protections for care workers in some of these contracts would strengthen the United States’ ability to defend people against disease outbreaks.

nodes.title: Societal Security: defense against disease outbreaks
nodes.claim_html: Strengthening this way to protect care workers and patients would help the United States defend people against disease outbreaks. The step from contract terms to national outbreak capacity has no source.

nodes.title: Enforceable anti-discrimination terms
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would contain anti-discrimination terms that workers can enforce through the contract and would otherwise lack or get later.

nodes.title: Concern: an easier way to enforce protection from discrimination
nodes.claim_html: A more accessible way to enforce protection from discrimination serves concern for vulnerable people and justice for people one does not know.

nodes.title: Tolerance: protection and practical terms for people who differ
nodes.claim_html: Enforceable protection from mistreatment for who people are or what they believe, or practical terms that adapt work to their differences, either one, serves accepting people who are different. The first needs the claim about anti-discrimination terms. The second needs the claim about terms that adapt work to differences.

nodes.title: Just cause or independent review
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would contain at least one of two discipline protections that workers would otherwise lack or get later: a rule that discipline needs just cause, or independent review of disputes with management. Either one is enough.

nodes.title: Concern: protection against unfair punishment
nodes.claim_html: Protection against unfair punishment, or a hearing outside the employer’s sole control, directly serves the concern that everyone receive just treatment.

nodes.title: From discipline protections to health
nodes.claim_html: Just-cause rules or independent review would give some workers tools to challenge unhealthy demands and unfair treatment, in ways that protect their physical or mental health.

nodes.title: Personal Security: tools to challenge unhealthy demands
nodes.claim_html: Tools to challenge unhealthy demands and unfair treatment protect workers’ control over their working conditions, which serves physical and mental health.

nodes.title: Schedule rules or rest periods that protect sleep
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would contain schedule rules or paid rest periods that protect workers’ sleep and recovery. Either one is enough.

nodes.title: Personal Security: sleep and recovery
nodes.claim_html: Schedule rules or paid rest periods, either one, protect sleep and recovery, which supports health and safety in ordinary working life.

nodes.title: Environmental terms in contracts
nodes.claim_html: Some of these contracts would contain enforceable environmental terms: a role for workers in environmental oversight, a right to stop work that threatens the environment, or green workplace programs. Any one is enough. The terms may be tied to workers’ own jobs, safety or health, or may be environment-only terms that an employer agrees to include.

nodes.title: Nature: environmental terms at work
nodes.claim_html: With environmental oversight, a right to stop work that threatens the environment, or green workplace programs in more first contracts, workers gain ways to find and enforce pollution rules, act before harm occurs and save resources. Any one is enough. Terms tied to workers’ jobs, safety or health count, and so do environment-only terms an employer agrees to; the binding process does not overcome an employer’s lawful refusal to bargain over environment-only topics. These terms serve caring for nature, defending it and protecting it from pollution.

nodes.title: Some pay gains
nodes.claim_html: Where the bill adds or brings forward a first contract, some newly organized workers would gain at least some pay.

nodes.title: Concern: pay for households facing hardship
nodes.claim_html: Pay gains serve workers and dependents who are vulnerable to financial hardship.

nodes.title: Personal Security: pay that buys health protection
nodes.claim_html: With some pay gain, workers can better afford medical care and healthy food, with benefits that reach beyond union members. That serves avoiding disease and protecting health.

nodes.title: Pay gains that reach beyond the workers
nodes.claim_html: Some of these pay gains would reach beyond the workers who receive them: through more investment in their children’s education, or through other employers raising pay to compete for workers. Either one is enough.

nodes.title: Concern: wider opportunities from pay gains
nodes.claim_html: Through children’s education or the spread of pay gains to other workers, the gains serve equal opportunities in life, including for people beyond one’s own circle.

nodes.title: From household income to a steadier economy
nodes.claim_html: Through some pay gains, or through protection of current pay during talks, more households would better withstand lost income, and that would make the wider U.S. economy steadier against swings caused by households’ financial problems.

nodes.title: Societal Security: household stability and a steadier economy
nodes.claim_html: A U.S. economy that better withstands swings caused by households’ financial problems supports a country that is secure and stable.

nodes.title: Payments that support national union political work
nodes.claim_html: By helping new private-sector unions reach first contracts, the bill would add at least some member payments to national labor organizations that use part of such money for political work.

nodes.title: Tradition: political work against inherited Christian teaching
nodes.claim_html: A firmer income and membership base strengthens organizations that work against inherited Christian teaching on unborn life, marriage and the understanding of male and female, against aid that makes Christian schooling affordable, and, if their stated positions still hold, against legal protection for serving others according to that faith. Preserving those teachings and practices gives a reason to oppose that effect.

nodes.title: Fewer first-contract strikes and lockouts
nodes.claim_html: The bill would reduce, at least somewhat, how often first-contract talks lead to a strike or lockout.

nodes.title: Concern: incomes and people who depend on services
nodes.claim_html: Fewer stoppages protect workers’ incomes and the vulnerable people, such as patients, who depend on their services.

nodes.title: Fewer first-contract hospital strikes
nodes.claim_html: Some of the avoided first-contract stoppages would be strikes at private hospitals, where strikes lower the quality of patient care.

nodes.title: Fewer stoppages at companies that support the military
nodes.claim_html: Some of the avoided first-contract stoppages would be at private companies whose work supports the military.

nodes.title: Personal Security: fewer hospital strikes
nodes.claim_html: Fewer first-contract strikes in private hospitals reduce a risk to the quality of care a person receives as a patient, which serves personal health and safety.

nodes.title: Societal Security: military support and medical care
nodes.claim_html: Fewer first-contract stoppages protect steady production, military support needed to defend citizens, and medical care needed to protect their lives. The medical-care part needs the claim about hospital strikes; the production and military part needs the claim about companies that support the military.

nodes.title: Panel-set rules that may not fit a workplace
nodes.claim_html: Because a panel can set binding terms, the bill adds at least some risk that a panel unfamiliar with a workplace or local market sets binding work or safety rules that do not fit it.

nodes.title: Ill-fitting safety rules
nodes.claim_html: The added risk of ill-fitting panel rules includes at least some risk that a panel sets binding safety rules that miss a workplace’s actual hazards, leaving workers more exposed to injury.

nodes.title: Concern: ill-fitting safety rules
nodes.claim_html: Making an ill-fitting safety rule binding despite workers’ objections puts the protection of people facing those hazards at risk.

nodes.title: Tolerance: local practices overridden
nodes.claim_html: Listening to different groups includes taking their local experience and working practices seriously. Binding terms set by people who may not know those practices, with no correction through objection, weaken that.

nodes.title: Ill-fitting rules at food and medical distributors
nodes.claim_html: The added risk of ill-fitting panel rules includes at least some risk that such rules are set at food or medical distributors and interfere with safe work there, putting essential deliveries at risk.

nodes.title: Societal Security: essential deliveries
nodes.claim_html: Panel rules that could interfere with safe work at food or medical distributors put essential deliveries at risk. Protecting those deliveries helps protect citizens and keep the country stable through crises.

nodes.title: Personal Security: final check on health and safety terms
nodes.claim_html: In a contract a panel sets, workers lose their final check on terms that affect their health and safety: ill-fitting safety rules, tiring schedules, sick leave or health coverage they find too limited. Keeping that check serves avoiding injury, recovering from illness, avoiding infection from sick coworkers, getting needed care and preventing crashes on roads they use. The safety-rule part also needs the claim about ill-fitting safety rules. The other parts need only the lost vote.

nodes.title: Risk of awards a small employer cannot sustain
nodes.claim_html: Because a panel can set binding terms, the bill adds at least some risk that a small employer receives an award it cannot sustain.

nodes.title: Concern: jobs and small owners’ income
nodes.claim_html: Costs a business cannot sustain threaten workers’ jobs and small owners’ income. That harms families with little money saved and closes opportunities to earn a living.

nodes.title: Small defense suppliers
nodes.claim_html: Some of the small employers at added risk would be defense suppliers, and an unaffordable award that closed one would reduce the supply of military parts and capabilities.

nodes.title: Societal Security: small defense suppliers
nodes.claim_html: An unaffordable award that closed a small defense supplier would threaten the supply of military parts and capabilities. Protecting those supplies serves a United States able to defend its citizens.

nodes.title: Less or slower help for unions that cannot buy private help
nodes.claim_html: The added required work would leave some workers whose unions cannot pay for private mediation with less or slower help from the reduced agency.

nodes.title: Concern: access to public help
nodes.claim_html: Equal opportunity requires protecting access to the help workers need to get pay and workplace protections. Added strain on a reduced agency leaves workers whose unions cannot buy private help with fewer ways around delay.

nodes.title: Resources drawn from essential-service disputes
nodes.claim_html: New required first-contract cases would draw some of the agency’s limited resources away from preventing disruptions to essential services such as power and health care.

nodes.title: Societal Security: essential services
nodes.claim_html: If new required cases draw on the resources used to prevent disruptions to power and health care, that risks weakening the state’s ability to keep essential services running and protect citizens.

nodes.title: More predictable labor costs and steadier economic activity
nodes.claim_html: Panel decisions that bind for two years and must weigh the business’s finances would make labor costs more predictable for some businesses, helping them plan staffing, spending and investment, and so supporting steadier economic activity across the United States.

nodes.title: Societal Security: steadier economic activity
nodes.claim_html: Steadier economic activity across the United States supports a country that is secure and stable.

nodes.title: Political pressure on panel appointments
nodes.claim_html: Where the agency fills empty panel seats, political pressure would shape some of its choices of panel members.

nodes.title: Concern: political influence over who decides terms
nodes.claim_html: Concern for just treatment gives a reason to protect workers from political influence over who decides their terms.

nodes.title: Hearing and lawsuit costs
nodes.claim_html: Required hearings, and legal challenges to the new process and to terms in imposed contracts, would use up some resources that employers or unions would otherwise spend on wages, benefits or representation.

nodes.title: Concern: money for wages, benefits and representation
nodes.claim_html: Preserving money for wages, benefits and representation, and the legal tools unions use, protects people with little individual power.

nodes.title: Limits on strikes for environmental demands
nodes.claim_html: A binding award would limit some strikes that workers could otherwise use to press environmental demands, either by ending first-contract bargaining or by imposing a strike ban.

nodes.title: Nature: acting together to defend nature
nodes.claim_html: Protecting workers’ way of acting together on the environment, including strikes to press green demands, serves taking part in defending nature. A binding award can limit that.

nodes.title: Pressure to settle early
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s timetable would press some workers to settle a first contract before they have fully understood and pressed their needs.

nodes.title: Concern: pressure to settle
nodes.claim_html: Protecting workers who depend on their pay and benefits includes a fair chance to understand and defend those needs. Pressure to accept less before they lose direct control threatens that protection.

nodes.title: Continuing union membership and racial resentment
nodes.claim_html: By keeping union relationships in place until an election, the bill would help some white workers keep union membership that reduces racial resentment.

nodes.title: Tolerance: cooperation across racial lines
nodes.claim_html: Cooperation across racial differences, through continuing union relationships, serves being tolerant toward all kinds of people and groups.

nodes.title: Tolerance: help with a difficult conversation
nodes.claim_html: Mediation help on request, and a shared way to settle a disagreement that remains, are ways of working with people despite disagreement.

nodes.title: Tolerance: a way around compromise
nodes.claim_html: Keeping the need for both groups to work through their differences serves listening to people with different views. A way around further compromise weakens that need.

nodes.title: Tradition: family needs in pay decisions
nodes.claim_html: Counting family needs in binding pay decisions supports the means to keep marriage and the roles of a father who provides and a mother who cares for children at home, an inherited family arrangement in this tradition.

nodes.title: Concern: protection against cuts during talks
nodes.claim_html: Protection against cuts while workers seek a contract protects people whose households cannot absorb lower pay or worse hours.

nodes.title: Personal Security: health coverage and safety rules kept during talks
nodes.claim_html: Keeping existing health coverage, sick leave and safety rules in place during talks serves personal health and safety.

nodes.title: Concern: raises held back after a deadlock
nodes.claim_html: Closing a way to higher pay after a deadlock, including in later contract talks, puts low-paid workers’ living standards and chances to get ahead at risk.

nodes.title: Concern: terms workers cannot reject by voting
nodes.claim_html: Letting workers reject terms they believe are harmful gives their needs a direct check on decisions that govern their income. Removing that safeguard in panel-set contracts weakens fair treatment.

nodes.title: Tolerance: members who disagree, and fee clauses
nodes.claim_html: Listening to people who disagree, and respecting dissent, give reasons to oppose losing members’ way to refuse approval and press negotiators to answer their objections. Separately, a fee clause in an imposed contract would make nonmembers pay for a bargaining voice they reject. Either route is enough.

nodes.title: Tradition: health coverage in line with faith
nodes.claim_html: For contracts a panel sets, the bill removes workers’ shared vote as a way to keep shared health coverage in line with inherited Christian teaching.

nodes.title: Nature: insisting on pollution-reducing terms
nodes.claim_html: Losing the vote removes a way for workers to insist on contract terms that reduce pollution and waste, which puts their ability to get such funding at risk.

nodes.title: Concern: a vote before representation ends
nodes.claim_html: Where an employer has evidence of lost majority support and the union has not asked for an election in time, workers keep collective representation until an election removes it. Requiring a vote before that protection ends gives workers a fairer process, which serves just treatment.

nodes.title: Tolerance: a continuing voice
nodes.claim_html: Hearing a group whose choice management dislikes puts acceptance despite disagreement into practice.

nodes.title: Concern: ending representation workers no longer want
nodes.claim_html: Just treatment includes respecting workers’ wishes about who speaks for them. Requiring an election adds an obstacle to ending representation they no longer want.

nodes.title: Tolerance: acting on workers’ rejection of a union
nodes.claim_html: Respecting people who disagree includes listening when workers reject a group’s claim to speak for them. Closing a lawful way to act on those changed wishes weakens that.

value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_BENEFITS: health coverage, paid sick or parental leave, pensions or other paid leave in more first contracts, and sooner (any one is enough)
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_COVERAGE: health coverage, or a lower share of health costs paid by workers, in more first contracts, and sooner
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_SICKLEAVE: paid sick leave in more first contracts, and sooner
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_TR_PARENTAL: paid parental leave in more first contracts, and the lower work and income pressure it brings for parents who follow the religious rule against abortion
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_HOURS: posted schedules and advance notice of schedules in more first contracts, making hours more predictable for caregivers
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_TR_WORSHIP: protection of existing Sunday and holiday work arrangements during talks, or new contract rules for advance schedule notice or schedule changes for religious holidays
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_PAYRULES: shared pay rules, such as published pay schedules, that make pay less open to bias against women and racial minorities
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_OPENINGS: posted job openings and a stated way to seek promotions in more first contracts
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_TRAINING: job training or help with tuition in more first contracts
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_OUTSIDE: contract limits on moving union-represented work to temporary staff, outside companies or managers
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_STAFFING: nurse-staffing rules in some private-hospital first contracts that keep staffing closer to safe levels for patients
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_DISCUSSION: regular workplace discussion or training about differences between people
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_SAFETY: enforceable safety rules in more first contracts, and sooner
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_SAFETY: enforceable safety rules in more first contracts, and sooner
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_OUTBREAK: a stronger U.S. ability to defend people against disease outbreaks, through infection protections for care workers
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_DISCRIMINATION: anti-discrimination terms that workers can enforce through their contract, an easier way than a legal claim
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_DIFFERENCES: enforceable protection from mistreatment for who people are or what they believe, or practical terms that adapt work to people’s differences
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_DISCIPLINE: a rule that discipline needs just cause, or independent review of disputes with management
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_CONTROL: tools to challenge unhealthy demands and unfair treatment that protect workers’ physical or mental health
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_SLEEP: schedule rules or paid rest periods that protect workers’ sleep and recovery
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNN_TERMS: environmental oversight, a right to stop work that threatens the environment, or green workplace programs in more first contracts
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_HARDSHIP: some pay gains for newly organized workers
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_PAYHEALTH: some pay gains that help workers afford medical care and healthy food
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_OPPORTUNITY: pay gains that reach beyond the workers who get them, through their children’s education or higher pay at other employers
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_HOUSEHOLDS: a U.S. economy steadier against swings caused by households’ money problems, through some pay gains or protection of current pay during talks
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_TR_POLITICAL: more member payments to national labor organizations that work against inherited Christian teaching on unborn life, marriage and male and female, against aid for Christian schooling and, if their stated positions still hold, against legal protection for serving others according to that faith
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_HOSPITAL: fewer first-contract strikes at private hospitals, where strikes lower the quality of patient care
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_STOPPAGES: fewer first-contract stoppages at private hospitals or at companies whose work supports the military
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_FIT: the added risk of binding panel safety rules that miss a workplace’s actual hazards
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_LOCAL: the added risk of binding rules set by a panel unfamiliar with a workplace or local market, which local groups could not correct by objecting
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_DELIVERIES: the added risk of ill-fitting panel rules at food or medical distributors that interfere with safe work and essential deliveries
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_VOTE: workers losing their final vote, in a contract a panel sets, on schedules, sick leave, health coverage and, given the added risk of ill-fitting safety rules, safety rules
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_UNAFFORDABLE: the added risk of an award a small employer cannot sustain, threatening jobs and owners’ income
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_DEFENSE: the added risk that an unaffordable award closes a small defense supplier, reducing the supply of military parts and capabilities
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_AGENCY: less or slower help from the reduced mediation agency for workers whose unions cannot pay for private help
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_ESSENTIAL: agency resources drawn away from preventing disruptions to essential services such as power and health care
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SES_PLANNING: more predictable labor costs that help businesses plan and support steadier U.S. economic activity
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_POLITICAL: political pressure on the agency’s choices of panel members
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_COSTS: hearing and lawsuit costs that use up money for wages, benefits or representation
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNN_STRIKES: limits on strikes that workers could use to press environmental demands
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_PRESSURE: pressure on workers to settle a first contract before they have fully understood and pressed their needs
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_RACIAL: less racial resentment among white workers who keep union membership
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_MEDIATION: mediation help on request, and a shared way to settle a disagreement that remains
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_COMPROMISE: a way for either side to go to a panel instead of further compromise
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_TR_FAMILYWAGE: a legal requirement that binding pay decisions count what workers need to support their families
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_CUTS: protection of current pay, hours and conditions against cuts while workers seek a contract
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_SEP_KEPT: keeping existing health coverage, sick leave and safety rules in place during talks
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_RAISES: a rule that stops employers from giving raises on their own after a deadlock, including in later contract talks
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_VOTE: workers losing their vote to reject a contract a panel sets
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_VOTE: members losing their vote to refuse a panel-set contract and press negotiators to answer objections, or, where an imposed contract includes one, a fee clause that makes nonmembers pay for a bargaining voice they reject
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_TR_COVERAGE: workers losing their shared vote on health coverage in a contract a panel sets, including coverage that may conflict with their faith
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNN_VOTE: workers losing their vote to insist on pollution-reducing terms in a contract a panel sets
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_ELECTION: a required worker election before an employer can end a union’s representation
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_VOICE: a continuing bargaining voice for a workers’ group that management opposes
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNC_ENDREP: a required election before workers can end representation they no longer want
value_subjects.HR5408_DT_V_UNT_REJECTION: closing an existing way, other than an election, to act on workers’ rejection of a union
